opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people have this picture of a research manager as someone who sits in meetings and moves boxes around on an org chart, and that's really not how I think about it. For me, the core of the job is making sure the team is working on the right problems, and then removing whatever is in the way of them making progress on those problems.

The first part, picking the right problems, is where I think a manager can have the most leverage. Especially in alignment, there are so many things you could work on that seem interesting or tractable, and a lot fewer that actually matter for the thing we care about, which is making sure that as these systems get more capable, they actually do what we want. So a big part of my role is constantly asking, "If this project succeeds, does it actually move the needle? Does it make the next generation of models meaningfully safer, or does it give us a technique that will scale?" And being willing to say, "This is cool, but let's not do it."

The second part is more about people. Researchers are often most productive when they have a clear sense of direction but a lot of autonomy in how they get there. So I try to set the goals and then mostly get out of the way. That means making sure they have the compute they need, that they're connected to the right people on other teams, that they're not blocked waiting on infrastructure, and that they get feedback quickly when something isn't working. A lot of research time gets wasted going down a path for three months that someone could have flagged in a week.

And then there's a piece that's specific to being at a lab like OpenAI, which is being a bridge. Alignment research doesn't happen in a vacuum. The techniques we develop are only useful if they actually get used on the models that ship. So part of my job is working with the people training the big models, understanding their constraints, and making the case for why a given safety approach is worth adopting. That's sometimes the hardest part, honestly, because it's less about the research and more about building trust and showing that the work is practically useful.

I'll also say I still try to stay close to the technical details. I don't think you can manage research well if you don't really understand what your team is doing. I'm not writing as much code as I used to, but I read a lot of the experiments, look at the results, and try to have opinions on them. If I lost that, I think I'd make worse calls about what to prioritize.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing the right problems, setting goals, and clearing blockers, but does not identify translating vague research questions into concrete tasks as a responsibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I see it, the job is really about enabling other people to do great research. It's not primarily about doing the research yourself anymore, which was honestly a bit of an adjustment for me when I moved into it. As an individual researcher, the thing you optimize for is: what's the most interesting problem I can make progress on? As a manager, the question becomes: what's the most important thing for the team to be working on, and how do I make sure the people on the team are set up to actually do it?

And I think there are a few pieces to that. One is setting direction. Alignment is a pretty wide-open area, and there are many things you could work on, and a lot of them aren't going to matter very much. So a big part of the job is thinking hard about which problems are actually on the critical path, and being willing to say, "we're going to focus on this and not on that," even when that's a bit uncomfortable because the other thing is also interesting.

The second piece is hiring, which I think people underrate a lot. The team you build is, in some sense, the main output. If you get really good people who care about the problem and have the right skills, a lot of the rest sort of takes care of itself. And the converse is also true: if you hire poorly, it's very hard to fix later.

And then the third piece is the day-to-day stuff: unblocking people, making sure they have compute and the infrastructure they need, giving feedback, helping people think through their research when they're stuck, and shielding them from a lot of the organizational noise so they can actually concentrate. A lot of that is pretty unglamorous, to be honest.

The thing I try to keep in mind is that at OpenAI specifically, we're in a position where the research isn't purely academic. The models we're building are going to be deployed, and the alignment work needs to actually connect to that. So part of the role is also being the bridge between the alignment research and the rest of the organization, making sure the things we learn actually make it into the systems that get built, and that the questions coming back from the people building those systems feed into what we work on. I think that's actually one of the more exciting parts of it, because you get a very tight feedback loop that you often don't get in a more academic setting.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing research priorities and helping researchers when they are stuck, but it does not identify translating vague research questions into concrete tasks as a managerial responsibility.

astra-6.text:
I think the core of the role is helping a team do good research. That means having a clear sense of what the most important questions are, but also giving people enough freedom to pursue their own ideas. Research is uncertain, so you can’t just lay out a detailed plan and expect everything to follow it.

A lot of the work is talking through ideas: What are we trying to learn? What experiment would actually tell us something? If we got this result, would it change what we do next? And then there’s building the team, giving people feedback, and making sure they have what they need.

There’s also a balance between doing research yourself and helping other people be more effective. You want to stay close enough to the technical work to have useful judgment, while recognising that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do is unblock somebody else.

r001.rationale: The response describes clarifying what the team is trying to learn and choosing an experiment that can answer it, communicating the work of turning research questions into concrete investigative tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a research manager’s job is to create the conditions for the team to do good research. That means helping people figure out which questions are most important, giving them useful feedback, and making sure they have the resources and collaborators they need.

There’s a balance here, because research is inherently uncertain. You can’t just lay out a detailed plan and expect it to work. You want researchers to have a lot of ownership and room to follow their ideas, while keeping a shared sense of what the team is trying to accomplish and why.

For alignment research, a big part of that is continually asking: if this project succeeds, how does it actually help us make AI systems safer? It’s easy to work on something interesting and technically challenging without having a clear answer to that question.

r001.rationale: The response says managers help researchers identify important questions, but does not say they translate vague research questions into concrete tasks.
